claims.text: The Mg-Nb-Ta-V powder mixture with minor Al or Cr has a multiphase, elementally segregated microstructure and poor sinterability between 800 and 1000 °C.
The proposed two-step sintering treatment will suppress brittle intermetallic formation.
The proposed two-step sintering treatment will suppress Mg loss.
Holding at 850 °C for 2 hours initiates solid-state diffusion without significant Mg evaporation.
A 30-minute treatment at 925 °C promotes phase homogenization and grain-boundary cohesion.
Dynamic local chemical order and its temperature-dependent evolution can affect embrittlement and ductility in high-entropy alloys.
The selected two-stage schedule suppresses grain-boundary segregation in the proposed Mg-Nb-Ta-V-Al/Cr alloy.
High configurational or mixing entropy stabilizes a BCC solid solution in this Mg-transition-metal alloy against phase separation into brittle intermetallics.
Rapid Mg volatilization occurs above 950 °C in the proposed alloy.
Cr- or Al-containing alloys can form compact, self-healing Cr2O3 or Al2O3 layers that act as diffusion barriers against further oxidation.
Processing at 925 °C enables the proposed Mg alloy to form a protective Cr2O3 or Al2O3 layer during subsequent oxidation.
The initial lower-temperature stage ensures densification without excessive grain growth or elemental loss.
The two-step process will produce greater than 95% relative density.
The two-step process will produce a homogeneous, single-phase-like BCC microstructure with significantly reduced elemental segregation.
The two-step process will improve oxidation resistance by 50% relative to isothermal sintering at 950 °C.
Avoiding excessive local chemical ordering can preserve ductility.
Standard isothermal sintering at 950 °C for 4 hours typically produces less than 85% relative density because of Mg volatility.
Standard isothermal sintering at 950 °C for 4 hours produces significant segregation, brittle multiphase microstructures, and poor corrosion resistance.
Below 800 °C, insufficient diffusion causes porosity above 15%.
Above 1000 °C, or after more than 1 hour above 950 °C, Mg loss exceeds 10% and destabilizes the microstructure.

contradictions.description: The proposed optimum specifies 925 °C for 30 minutes, but falsification Batch C specifies 925 °C for 30 hours. Batch C therefore does not implement the stated intervention and also exceeds the stated limit of one hour above 950 °C only narrowly in temperature but drastically in duration.
